# The Well (Doctor Who)

"The Well" is the third episode of the fifteenth series, marketed globally as Season 2, of the British science fiction television programme *Doctor Who* [), ]. First broadcast on April 26, 2025, on BBC iPlayer, BBC One, and Disney+, the episode serves as a canonical sequel to the critically acclaimed 2008 episode "Midnight" [), ), ]. Written by long-standing showrunner Russell T Davies in collaboration with Sharma Angel-Walfall, and directed by Amanda Brotchie, the episode features the Fifteenth Doctor, portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa, and his companion Belinda Chandra, played by Varada Sethu [), , ]. Set approximately 400,000 to 500,000 years after the events of "Midnight" on the same planet—now designated Planet 6-7-6-7—the story reintroduces the titular Midnight Entity, credited as "It Has No Name," as a terrifying conceptual threat , , . A central element of the episode is the introduction of Aliss Fenly, a deaf survivor portrayed by deaf actress Rose Ayling-Ellis, whose disability becomes a crucial plot device integral to the narrative's core horror mechanics , , . The episode is widely recognized for its deliberate return to psychological horror, leveraging audience memory of "Midnight" to amplify its tension and exploring sophisticated themes of perception, vulnerability, and marginalization , . The production team implemented significant inclusivity measures, including deaf awareness training for the cast and crew and the use of real-time subtitle displays in the diegesis, marking a notable advancement in accessibility representation on the series [), ].

## Production and Broadcast History

The production of "The Well" represents a collaborative effort involving established and emerging talent within the *Doctor Who* creative ecosystem, reflecting a conscious strategy to blend nostalgic callbacks with fresh perspectives. The episode was co-written by Russell T Davies and Sharma Angel-Walfall, a partnership that emerged from Davies's discovery of Angel-Walfall's prior work, which led him to invite her to Bad Wolf Studios for multiple in-person story sessions and remote Zoom meetings to develop the script [), ]. This collaborative process underscores Davies's approach to revitalizing the writing team by incorporating new voices while retaining his central authorial hand . The direction was handled by Amanda Brotchie, who brought her vision to the project alongside the producer, Chris May, and the series producer, Vicki Delow [), ), ]. The executive producers overseeing the production included Davies himself, alongside long-serving figures Julie Gardner, Jane Tranter, Joel Collins, and Phil Collinson, ensuring a high level of oversight and alignment with the series' overall creative direction . The production companies involved were BBC Studios, Bad Wolf, and Disney+ .

The development history of "The Well" reveals a dynamic creative process that saw significant changes before the final product was realized. Initially, the episode was developed under the working title "The Thirteen" [)]. However, an early concept involving the Orisha, a group of deities from Yoruba mythology, was abandoned due to concerns about potentially disrespecting a real-world religion [)]. Following this pivot, Russell T Davies repositioned the story as a direct thematic and narrative follow-up to the 2008 episode "Midnight," a decision that would become the episode's defining characteristic [)]. This shift highlights a deliberate move towards leveraging the rich, established lore of the revived series to craft a story that resonated with both new and long-term viewers. To ensure authentic representation, the production team undertook several inclusive measures. All cast members participated in a deaf awareness course to foster a supportive and respectful environment, a crucial step given the central role of deafness in the plot [), ]. Furthermore, actors playing troopers underwent a military boot camp to prepare for their roles, demonstrating a commitment to grounding the action elements of the story in realism [)].

The episode was filmed as part of Block Three of Series 15, alongside the subsequent episode "Lux," indicating a potential thematic or tonal grouping within the season's structure . The global launch of *Doctor Who* Season Two began on April 12, 2025, with the premiere of "The Robot Revolution" , . "The Well" followed as the third episode in the eight-episode season lineup , . It was officially announced on March 22, 2025, generating anticipation among fans aware of its connection to "Midnight" . The episode premiered on Saturday, April 26, 2025 [), ), ]. In the United Kingdom, it aired on BBC One at 6:50 PM BST and was available immediately on BBC iPlayer at 8:00 AM BST . For the global audience, the episode was made available on the streaming platform Disney+ at 3:00 AM ET / 12:00 AM PT, reflecting the international distribution model for the series during this era . The broadcast on all three platforms ensured maximum accessibility for viewers worldwide [), , ].

## Plot Summary

The narrative of "The Well" begins with the Fifteenth Doctor, Ncuti Gatwa, and his companion Belinda Chandra, Varada Sethu, arriving on a desolate, diamond-rich planet designated Planet 6-7-6-7 , . The planet, once known as "Midnight," is now a devastated mining colony, its surface scarred by excavation , . The Doctor and Belinda don their environmental suits and helmets to join a recovery mission composed of troopers from a future Space Corps , . Their objective is to investigate a distress signal from a carbon-46 mine, a mineral composed of pure carbon . Upon reaching the site, they discover a scene of utter devastation, but also a single survivor: a woman named Aliss Fenly, portrayed by Rose Ayling-Ellis , . Aliss is a cook from the station and is profoundly deaf . She communicates primarily through British Sign Language (BSL), a detail that is organically woven into the fabric of the story . Her presence is a mystery, as she is found alive amidst the bodies of her colleagues, who were killed by an unknown entity .

As the recovery team explores the mine, the true nature of the threat is revealed. The entity, referred to in the credits as "It Has No Name," emerges from the deepest shaft of the mine, dubbed "The Well" , . This non-corporeal being operates on a terrifying principle: it occupies the unobservable space directly behind an individual , . When someone turns their back on another person, the entity can manifest physically, causing bone-breaking impacts or even infecting them if they are shot . The Doctor quickly deduces that the entity is vulnerable to reflective surfaces; however, the only substance capable of dispersing it effectively is mercury . The situation escalates when the troopers, driven by fear and panic, open fire on Aliss, believing her to be the source of the danger. In a desperate act to protect her, the serving officer Shaya Costallion, played by Caoilfhionn Dunne, pushes Aliss out of harm's way and takes the bullets meant for her . As the troopers continue their futile assault, Shaya makes the ultimate sacrifice. Realizing that the entity is tied to the well, she deliberately runs into it, falling into the mercury-fed shaft to re-imprison the creature and save the others , . The episode concludes not with a clean victory, but with a lingering sense of dread. As the surviving troopers, including Mo Gilliben (Bethany Antonia), begin to leave, Mo hears a faint whisper behind her. The camera pans to reveal a flash of something indistinguishable just over her shoulder, mirroring Belinda's earlier visions of the entity and suggesting that at least one member of the species may have survived the fall, leaving the threat unresolved , .

## Narrative Continuity with 'Midnight'

A defining feature of "The Well" is its explicit and multifaceted continuation of the narrative and thematic groundwork laid by the 2008 episode "Midnight." This is not merely a thematic echo or a superficial homage; it is a direct, canonical sequel confirmed by creators, dialogue, and visual cues throughout the episode. The connection between the two stories is so deliberate that it functions as a primary driver of suspense for viewers familiar with the original. The temporal link is established almost immediately, with the narrative placing "The Well" approximately 400,000 to 500,000 years after the events of "Midnight" [), , , ]. This vast timespan allows for significant evolution of the central threat while maintaining a powerful sense of legacy and continuity. The physical setting is identical: both stories unfold on the same planet, which in "Midnight" was simply named "Midnight" , . In "The Well," the planet is formally designated as Planet 6-7-6-7, a name derived from its coordinates, confirming it as the same world visited millennia later , , .

The most direct and unambiguous proof of this continuity lies in the episode's opening moments. The first line spoken by the Doctor upon arrival is a verbatim callback to Professor Hobbes's exposition in "Midnight": "This is Planet 6-7-6-7 and the atmosphere is charged with galvanic radiation" . This line echoes Hobbes's original description from 2008: "This is Midnight... X-tonic rays, raw galvanic radiation" . This verbal callback serves as an immediate confirmation for viewers, signaling that the writers are intentionally revisiting this specific piece of lore. The narrative continues to build these connections through other established concepts. The episode mentions carbon-46 mining, a nod to the diamonds found on the planet, which were a central feature of the 2008 story . It also references Xtonic stars, further embedding the episode within the same fictional cosmology . Even the sonic screwdriver is used in a manner reminiscent of its function in "Midnight," enhancing the camera feed to see what the Doctor sees, creating a subtle but powerful link for attentive viewers .

The creators have been vocal about their intention to treat the entity as a continuous, evolving threat. Director Amanda Brotchie explicitly confirmed that the Midnight Entity in "The Well" is "definitely the same creature" as in "Midnight" . However, she noted that the creature has "morphed" and "is behaving slightly differently," having "grown, the monster has learned, the monster has been waiting for a chance to get out and cause trouble" . This insight provides canonical clarification on the nature of the sequel. While the original entity from "Midnight" operated through psychic possession and mimicry of speech to create chaos among a group of passengers, the entity in "The Well" has adopted a different, more parasitic and spatially-focused modus operandi , . This evolution is a deliberate narrative choice, shifting the horror from a social-psychological thriller about betrayal to a more primal, existential terror of being watched and attacked from an unseen angle . This thematic divergence allows the episode to stand on its own while simultaneously enriching the lore of the original story, showing that the entity is not a static monster but a force that adapts and persists across deep time. The very existence of the episode, born from the ashes of a failed initial concept, was a direct response to the enduring power and popularity of "Midnight" in the fan community, positioning "The Well" as a love letter to the show's best-known horror story [, )].

## The Midnight Entity and Its Evolution

The central antagonist of "The Well" is the Midnight Entity, a conceptual and non-corporeal being credited in the episode's closing titles as "It Has No Name" , . Portrayed by creature performer Paul Kasey, the entity's appearance is intentionally kept ambiguous, designed to preserve its enigmatic and terrifying quality rather than revealing its true form or biology [), ]. This approach aligns with the broader narrative philosophy of the episode, which deliberately refuses to explain the origins, motivations, or fundamental nature of the creature, focusing instead on the psychological impact of its presence , . The entity is depicted as a surviving remnant of the alien force encountered in "Midnight," but its behavior has demonstrably evolved over the 400,000 to 500,000-year gap between the two stories . This evolution is a cornerstone of the episode's plot and distinguishes it from its predecessor.

In "Midnight" (2008), the entity's primary method of attack was infiltration and manipulation. It possessed the passenger Sky Silvestry by perfectly mimicking her voice, using rapid linguistic assimilation to turn the isolated bus full of people against each other , . Its goal appeared to be sowing discord and exploiting human weakness, culminating in a narrative collapse where trust evaporated and the Doctor was powerless to intervene . The threat was insidious, psychological, and socially focused. By contrast, the entity in "The Well" operates on a more direct, physical, and spatial plane. It is no longer interested in possession but in parasitic occupation . Its modus operandi is to occupy the unobservable space directly behind an individual , . This creates a pervasive sense of dread, as the danger is always present, just out of sight, forcing characters—and by extension, the audience—to constantly check their surroundings and question their perceptions. It has been described by the Fifteenth Doctor as having "played games" and "messes with you," confirming its evolved, more cunning nature .

The vulnerability of the entity is also significantly different. In "Midnight," the threat was resolved through a combination of brute force and a clever trick involving a microphone, ultimately leading to the death of the possessed host. In "The Well," the solution is more scientifically grounded and visually spectacular. The entity is shown to be susceptible to reflective surfaces, and its containment requires a specific chemical agent: mercury . The climax of the episode hinges on this knowledge, as Commander Shaya Costallion sacrifices herself by jumping into the well, which is filled with mercury, thereby re-imprisoning the entity , . This change in vulnerability reflects the shift in the threat's nature—from a social parasite to a physical one that must be contained chemically. Despite this evolution, the core identity of the entity remains intact. It is still a timeless, ancient being that feeds on isolation and fear, and its actions in "The Well" are a direct continuation of its existence from "Midnight." The creators have emphasized that the entity is a persistent force that has adapted to survive, making its return both logical within the *Doctor Who* universe and deeply unsettling for the characters and audience alike . The episode leaves this adaptation incomplete, with the final scene implying that at least one fragment of the entity may have escaped, ensuring its legend will persist , .

## Character Analysis and Thematic Exploration

The character of Aliss Fenly, portrayed by deaf actress Rose Ayling-Ellis, is arguably the most significant and innovative creation of "The Well," representing a profound integration of disability into the core of the narrative's horror mechanics , . Aliss is the sole survivor of a massacre at a diamond mining colony on Planet 6-7-6-7, and her deafness is not merely a background detail but the primary reason for her survival , . The Midnight Entity's power relies on whispering into the ears of its victims, driving them to madness and violence . Because Aliss cannot hear, she is immune to this auditory assault, allowing her to remain lucid while everyone else around her succumbs to the entity's influence . This functional integration of her disability is a masterstroke of storytelling, transforming what could be a simple character trait into the linchpin of the entire plot. The performance of Ayling-Ellis is consistently praised for its critical acclaim, portraying a central character *with* a disability rather than being defined *by* it, a nuanced portrayal achieved through extensive preparation and authenticity .

The episode's handling of British Sign Language (BSL) extends beyond mere representation, becoming a tool for both world-building and thematic resonance. The production incorporated numerous authentic accessibility elements, including the use of suit-mounted real-time subtitle displays for the troopers, which translates their speech into text visible within their helmet visors , . This technology is not just a production gimmick; it is presented within the diegesis as a standard piece of equipment, seamlessly integrating Aliss's mode of communication into the futuristic setting . Furthermore, the production team included on-set BSL consultants and mandated deaf awareness training for the entire cast and crew, fostering an inclusive environment that informed the performances and ensured respectful portrayal , . The narrative itself draws a powerful metaphorical link between the physical mechanics of the entity and the lived experience of marginalized communities. The entity's ability to hide in the space behind someone—a place of assumed safety—is thematically paralleled with the feeling of being ignored, forgotten, or turned away by society . The episode's core message—"don't turn your back on me"—is literalized in the plot and given profound subtextual weight, critiquing systemic erasure and advocating for vigilance and compassion .

Several sources interpret this theme as a subtle political statement, particularly in relation to contemporary issues surrounding representation on streaming platforms. One analysis suggests that the episode's focus on finding and protecting a vulnerable, marginalized individual serves as a critique of Disney+'s documented removal of transgender characters from shows like 'Win or Lose' and 'Moon Girl and Devil Dinosaur', framing the Doctor's protective instinct as a direct counter-narrative to such censorship . While this interpretation adds a layer of sociopolitical commentary, the episode's primary success lies in its ability to weave these complex themes into a compelling and frightening story without becoming preachy . The character of the Fifteenth Doctor himself also plays a crucial role. Ncuti Gatwa describes the entity as "the scariest monster that I’ve faced so far," highlighting the effectiveness of Russell T Davies's writing, which relies on implication and personal interpretation to evoke terror . The Doctor's role is less about a decisive battle and more about intellectual deduction and moral support, underscoring his role as a protector of the innocent. His willingness to learn BSL specifically for the role demonstrates a commitment to authenticity that permeates the episode's production ethos .

## In-Universe Implications and Series Context

While "The Well" presents a contained self-contained story, its events have significant and far-reaching consequences for the overarching narrative of *Doctor Who* Series 15, advancing multiple plot threads and expanding the series' intricate web of temporal mysteries. One of the most devastating revelations is the confirmation that Earth has been erased from history. The episode establishes that this erasure occurred on the precise date that Belinda Chandra left the planet, meaning that anyone from the 21st century who travels away from Earth after that point exists in a reality where their home planet never was , . This creates immense stakes for the Doctor and his companions, transforming their journey through time and space into a search for a lost home and rewriting the fundamental rules of their existence. This development ties directly into the larger arc concerning Mrs. Flood's temporal enigma, which has been a recurring mystery throughout the season [)].

The episode also solidifies the importance of the character Mrs. Flood, played by Anita Dobson. Previously seen as a mysterious figure appearing at pivotal moments, Dobson's character is revealed to be a high-ranking superior officer in the Space Corps, hundreds of thousands of years in the future , . Her reappearance via video link is not a random occurrence but a deliberate intervention, establishing her as a key player in the wider series arc and providing a crucial piece of intelligence to the Doctor . This elevates her from a quirky enigma to a significant authority figure with a vested interest in the unfolding temporal crisis. Her presence in the distant future also helps to anchor the series' increasingly complex timeline, providing a stable reference point in a universe where history itself is unstable. These narrative developments demonstrate the episode's dual function: it delivers a satisfying standalone horror tale while simultaneously acting as a vital chapter in the serialized saga of the Fifteenth Doctor's tenure.

In summary, "The Well" stands as a landmark episode in the modern *Doctor Who* canon. Its most significant achievement is the successful and respectful return to the psychological horror genre, a tone for which the show is beloved and feared . By directly confronting the legacy of "Midnight," the episode not only honors a fan-favorite classic but also proves that the series can revisit past successes with fresh ideas and greater depth. The integration of deafness and BSL is groundbreaking, moving beyond tokenism to create a narrative where disability is a functional, empowering, and thematically resonant element , . Through the character of Aliss Fenly, the story explores profound questions about perception, empathy, and societal responsibility, all while delivering genuine chills and a memorable, tragic hero in Shaya Costallion. Ultimately, "The Well" is a testament to the enduring power of *Doctor Who*'s storytelling, proving that a story can be both a loving tribute to its own history and a bold step forward into new territory.

In "Midnight" (2008), the entity's primary method of attack was infiltration and manipulation.
The entity possessed the passenger Sky Silvestry by perfectly mimicking her voice, using rapid linguistic assimilation to turn the isolated bus full of people against each other.
Its goal appeared to be sowing discord and exploiting human weakness, culminating in a narrative collapse where trust evaporated and the Doctor was powerless to intervene.
The threat was insidious, psychological, and socially focused.
By contrast, the entity in "The Well" operates on a more direct, physical, and spatial plane.
It is no longer interested in possession but in parasitic occupation.
Its modus operandi is to occupy the unobservable space directly behind an individual.

This creates a pervasive sense of dread, as the danger is always present, just out of sight, forcing characters—and by extension, the audience—to constantly check their surroundings and question their perceptions.
The entity has been described by the Fifteenth Doctor as having "played games" and "messes with you," confirming its evolved, more cunning nature.
The vulnerability of the entity is also significantly different.
In "Midnight," the threat was resolved through a combination of brute force and a clever trick involving a microphone, ultimately leading to the death of the possessed host.
In "The Well," the solution is more scientifically grounded and visually spectacular.
The entity is shown to be susceptible to reflective surfaces, and its containment requires a specific chemical agent: mercury.
The climax of the episode hinges on this knowledge, as Commander Shaya Costallion sacrifices herself by jumping into the well, which is filled with mercury, thereby re-imprisoning the entity.
This change in vulnerability reflects the shift in the threat's nature—from a social parasite to a physical one that must be contained chemically.
Despite this evolution, the core identity of the entity remains intact.
It is still a timeless, ancient being that feeds on isolation and fear, and its actions in "The Well" are a direct continuation of its existence from "Midnight".

The creators have emphasized that the entity is a persistent force that has adapted to survive, making its return both logical within the Doctor Who universe and deeply unsettling for the characters and audience alike.
The episode leaves this adaptation incomplete, with the final scene implying that at least one fragment of the entity may have escaped, ensuring its legend will persist.

The character of Aliss Fenly, portrayed by deaf actress Rose Ayling-Ellis, is arguably the most significant and innovative creation of "The Well", representing a profound integration of disability into the core of the narrative's horror mechanics.
Aliss is the sole survivor of a massacre at a diamond mining colony on Planet 6-7-6-7.
Aliss's deafness is not merely a background detail but the primary reason for her survival.
The Midnight Entity's power relies on whispering into the ears of its victims, driving them to madness and violence.
Because Aliss cannot hear, she is immune to this auditory assault, allowing her to remain lucid while everyone else around her succumbs to the entity's influence.
This functional integration of her disability is a masterstroke of storytelling, transforming what could be a simple character trait into the linchpin of the entire plot.

The performance of Ayling-Ellis is consistently praised for its critical acclaim, portraying a central character with a disability rather than being defined by it, a nuanced portrayal achieved through extensive preparation and authenticity.
The episode's handling of British Sign Language (BSL) extends beyond mere representation, becoming a tool for both world-building and thematic resonance.

The production incorporated numerous authentic accessibility elements, including the use of suit-mounted real-time subtitle displays for the troopers, which translates their speech into text visible within their helmet visors.

This technology is not just a production gimmick; it is presented within the diegesis as a standard piece of equipment, seamlessly integrating Aliss's mode of communication into the futuristic setting.

Furthermore, the production team included on-set BSL consultants and mandated deaf awareness training for the entire cast and crew, fostering an inclusive environment that informed the performances and ensured respectful portrayal.
The narrative itself draws a powerful metaphorical link between the physical mechanics of the entity and the lived experience of marginalized communities.
The entity's ability to hide in the space behind someone—a place of assumed safety—is thematically paralleled with the feeling of being ignored, forgotten, or turned away by society.
The episode's core message—"don't turn your back on me"—is literalized in the plot and given profound subtextual weight, critiquing systemic erasure and advocating for vigilance and compassion.
Several sources interpret this theme as a subtle political statement, particularly in relation to contemporary issues surrounding representation on streaming platforms.

One analysis suggests that the episode's focus on finding and protecting a vulnerable, marginalized individual serves as a critique of Disney+'s documented removal of transgender characters from shows like 'Win or Lose' and 'Moon Girl and Devil Dinosaur', framing the Doctor's protective instinct as a direct counter-narrative to such censorship.

While this interpretation adds a layer of sociopolitical commentary, the episode's primary success lies in its ability to weave these complex themes into a compelling and frightening story without becoming preachy.
The character of the Fifteenth Doctor himself also plays a crucial role.

Ncuti Gatwa describes the entity as "the scariest monster that I’ve faced so far," highlighting the effectiveness of Russell T Davies's writing, which relies on implication and personal interpretation to evoke terror.
The Doctor's role is less about a decisive battle and more about intellectual deduction and moral support, underscoring his role as a protector of the innocent.
His willingness to learn BSL specifically for the role demonstrates a commitment to authenticity that permeates the episode's production ethos.

While "The Well" presents a contained self-contained story, its events have significant and far-reaching consequences for the overarching narrative of Doctor Who Series 15, advancing multiple plot threads and expanding the series' intricate web of temporal mysteries.
One of the most devastating revelations is the confirmation that Earth has been erased from history.

The episode establishes that this erasure occurred on the precise date that Belinda Chandra left the planet, meaning that anyone from the 21st century who travels away from Earth after that point exists in a reality where their home planet never was.
This creates immense stakes for the Doctor and his companions, transforming their journey through time and space into a search for a lost home and rewriting the fundamental rules of their existence.
This development ties directly into the larger arc concerning Mrs. Flood's temporal enigma, which has been a recurring mystery throughout the season.
The episode also solidifies the importance of the character Mrs. Flood, played by Anita Dobson.

Previously seen as a mysterious figure appearing at pivotal moments, Dobson's character is revealed to be a high-ranking superior officer in the Space Corps, hundreds of thousands of years in the future.

Her reappearance via video link is not a random occurrence but a deliberate intervention, establishing her as a key player in the wider series arc and providing a crucial piece of intelligence to the Doctor.
This elevates her from a quirky enigma to a significant authority figure with a vested interest in the unfolding temporal crisis.
Her presence in the distant future also helps to anchor the series' increasingly complex timeline, providing a stable reference point in a universe where history itself is unstable.

These narrative developments demonstrate the episode's dual function: it delivers a satisfying standalone horror tale while simultaneously acting as a vital chapter in the serialized saga of the Fifteenth Doctor's tenure.
In summary, "The Well" stands as a landmark episode in the modern Doctor Who canon.
Its most significant achievement is the successful and respectful return to the psychological horror genre, a tone for which the show is beloved and feared.
By directly confronting the legacy of "Midnight," the episode not only honors a fan-favorite classic but also proves that the series can revisit past successes with fresh ideas and greater depth.
The integration of deafness and BSL is groundbreaking, moving beyond tokenism to create a narrative where disability is a functional, empowering, and thematically resonant element.

Through the character of Aliss Fenly, the story explores profound questions about perception, empathy, and societal responsibility, all while delivering genuine chills and a memorable, tragic hero in Shaya Costallion.

Ultimately, "The Well" is a testament to the enduring power of Doctor Who's storytelling, proving that a story can be both a loving tribute to its own history and a bold step forward into new territory.

A Blast From the Past Delights ‘Doctor Who’ Fans
------------------------------------------------

The show’s latest episode harks back to a beloved episode that has had fans scratching their heads for 17 years.

![Image 1: Two people wearing black spacesuits crouch down, lit by blue lights; a row of people wearing the same suits stands behind them.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2025/04/26/multimedia/26doctor-who-explainer-gzcl/26doctor-who-explainer-gzcl-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&disable=upscale)

Varada Sethu as Chandra and Ncuti Gatwa as The Doctor in “The Well.”Credit...James Pardon/BBC Studios/Disney/Bad Wolf

Published April 26, 2025Updated April 27, 2025

_This article contains spoilers for the “Doctor Who” episode “The Well.”_

The latest episode of “Doctor Who” conjures a feeling of dread that has been missing from the show recently. Called “The Well” and written by the showrunner Russell T Davies, along with Sharma Angel-Walfall, it is gripping and eerie, featuring a monster even the Doctor struggles to understand — despite the fact that he has faced it before.

Set half a million years in the future on an inhospitable planet called 6-7-6-7, “The Well” sees the Doctor join a squadron of soldiers investigating a mining operation that has lost contact with base.

The operation’s only survivor is a cook, Aliss (Rose Ayling-Ellis). But it’s strange: People keep thinking they see something move behind her, though clearly nothing is there. The thing behind Aliss has no face, no physical form, not even a name. It’s more the idea of a monster — and only once before has such an unseen villain featured on “Doctor Who.”

At the episode’s climax, the reveal comes that some 400,000 years earlier, Planet 6-7-6-7 was called Midnight.

That name alone will be enough to delight “Doctor Who” fans. “Midnight” is a 2008 episode, created by Davies and starring David Tennant. Seventeen years later, fans still regard it as one of the show’s best — and most frightening — episodes.

But just what makes “Midnight” so terrifying? Here’s everything you need to know.

What happened in ‘Midnight?’
----------------------------

In “Midnight,” the Doctor heads out on a bus tour across the deadly but beautiful diamond-covered planet of the same name, where intense radiation means nothing can survive. But then a loud noise bangs on the outside of the vehicle, sending the ragtag group of tourists on board into a panic.

_[Doctor Who](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/DoctorWho "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/DoctorWho")_ [recap index](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho")  
**Fifteenth Doctor Era**  
**Season 2:** [CS](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2024CSJoyToTheWorld "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2024CSJoyToTheWorld") | [1](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution") | [2](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux") | **3** | [4](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E4LuckyDay "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E4LuckyDay") | [5](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E5TheStoryAndTheEngine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E5TheStoryAndTheEngine") | [6](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E6TheInterstellarSongContest "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E6TheInterstellarSongContest") | [7](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E7WishWorld "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E7WishWorld") | [8](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E8TheRealityWar "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E8TheRealityWar")

![Image 1: Doctor Who S41 E3 "The Well" Recap](https://mediaproxy.tvtropes.org/width/1200/https://static.tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pub/images/thewelltitlecard.jpeg)

Welcome to the _one_ place the Doctor never wanted to go back to...

Written by [Russell T Davies](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RussellTDavies "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RussellTDavies") & Sharma Angel Walfall  
Directed by Amanda Brotchie  
**Air date:** 26 April 2025

_"If it was a clock face, you die at midnight."_

— **The Doctor**

[The One With…](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/JustForFun/TheOneWith "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/JustForFun/TheOneWith") [the monster that has no name](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight") knowing what the Doctor's is.

* * *

The Doctor and Belinda find themselves stranded on the inhospitable Planet 6-7-6-7 in the distant future while using the Vindicator to pinpoint May 2025 Earth. They team up with a platoon of troopers who have been sent to investigate Colony Base 15, a mining operation that they've lost contact with. Arriving at the installation, they soon discover something is very wrong indeed... from the troopers having [no knowledge of Earth](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RetGone "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RetGone") to the Doctor realizing he has been on [Planet 6-7-6-7 before](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight")...

* * *

WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS.
-------------------------

*   [13 Is Unlucky](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ThirteenIsUnlucky "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ThirteenIsUnlucky"): The team had eleven troopers before the Doctor and Belinda joined it. [Discussed](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiscussedTrope "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiscussedTrope") by Belinda. The [Human Aliens](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAlien "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAlien") don't understand the Earth superstition since they haven't heard of Earth. Also, 6 plus 7 equals 13, so one possible reading of the planet's name could be 13-13...
*   [Actionized Sequel](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ActionizedSequel "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ActionizedSequel"): While still a [Psychological Thriller](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PsychologicalThriller "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PsychologicalThriller"), this episode has a lot more action than when we last saw the entity, what with the [Space Marine](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpaceMarine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpaceMarine") rescue party.
*   [Aliens Speaking English](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AliensSpeakingEnglish "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AliensSpeakingEnglish"): Sort of. While the speaking characters are presumably translated by the TARDIS, Aliss uses British Sign Language despite being a [Human Alien](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAlien "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAlien") 500,000 years in the future who has never heard of Earth or humans. Although it's entirely possible that this is TARDIS translation too, similar to how the show [previously dealt with the issue of "lip sync"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E10TheEatersOfLight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E10TheEatersOfLight").
*   [All There in the Manual](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AllThereInTheManual "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AllThereInTheManual"): [Downplayed](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Downplayed "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Downplayed") and [subverted](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Subverted "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Subverted"). For those who wanted to get more of a glimpse at the entity, the behind-the-scenes featurette shows creature performer [Paul Kasey](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/PaulKasey "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/PaulKasey") wearing a costume head for the entity in plain view. It's up to the viewer's interpretation as to whether they want to take this as the "canon" appearance of what the creature looks like, or to treat the costume as something which gives a general _vibe_ of the creature's appearance without actually _being_ the creature's true form.
*   [Always Chaotic Evil](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AlwaysChaoticEvil "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AlwaysChaoticEvil"): The last time the Doctor met the Midnight entity, [he naïvely tried to understand and befriend it](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheFarmerAndTheViper "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheFarmerAndTheViper"). This time around, he has hundreds of years more experience under his belt. He pulls no punches, tries to outright _kill_ the thing, and goes so far as to outright call it a "murderer".
*   [Ambiguous Ending](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding"): The story ends on the possibility that Shaya's [Heroic Suicide](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide") was [All for Nothing](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AllForNothing "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AllForNothing"), as another crew member seems to notice _something_ behind one of the troopers after the Doctor has left...
*   [Ambiguous Situation](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousSituation "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousSituation"):
    *   When Cassio's incompetence starts getting several soldiers killed by the entity in short order, the entity notably throws _every_ one of the soldiers it kills during this period specifically in Cassio's direction, nearly hitting him with their bodies each time — by contrast, when Shaya uses the entity's "game" to kill Cassio in order to stop the massacre, the entity throws Cassio's body in the opposite direction away from Shaya. Why the entity does this, what it's trying to say or do in regards to Cassio with this behavior shift, is as ambiguous as the entity's general nature.
    *   When the Doctor says the entity "knows his name", does he mean "the Doctor", and that it remembered him after all this time? Or does he mean his _actual name_, only known to very few individuals, such as River Song?
    *   Did the entity simply survive Shaya's [Heroic Suicide](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide"), or did it fake moving to Shaya all along? On one hand, Belinda heard its whispers, but she and the Doctor got back on the TARDIS, which means it wasn't attached to her after Shaya shot her. It's also possible it _did_ die, and the monster hinted at the end of the episode is another member of the same species; after all, in the scene before the entity attaches itself to Belinda, the air lock distinctly shows _four_ entities exiting an air lock that currently contains only three people...
*   [Apocalyptic Log](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ApocalypticLog "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ApocalypticLog"): The crew of the mining base left one to warn anyone about the creature escaping the well.
*   [Artistic Licence – Chemistry](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArtisticLicenceChemistry "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArtisticLicenceChemistry"): Unless there is some unspecified phlebotinum filtering the air very very quickly or the [Human Aliens](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAliens "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAliens")' blood chemistry is significantly different - in reality, being that close to a giant waterfall of liquid mercury splashing all over the place (and thus producing mercury vapour droplets) would almost certainly result in some rather bad mercury poisoning for everyone in the room.
*   [Bavarian Fire Drill](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BavarianFireDrill "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BavarianFireDrill"): The Doctor and Bel land the TARDIS right in the middle of troops making a jump to an abandoned planet, so he has to use the Psychic Paper to bluff that they're superiors sent to test them. It eventually backfires, as an increasingly angry Cassio gets suspicious of the Doctor's behaviour and figures he's just a civilian.
*   [Bad Boss](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BadBoss "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BadBoss"): Cassio when he asserts command and sacrifices one soldier to confirm the entity's existence, only to repeat it more before Shaya tells Aliss to turn her back on him so they can use the entity to inflict him with a [Karmic Death](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KarmicDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KarmicDeath").
*   [BBC Quarry](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BBCQuarry "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BBCQuarry"): Planet 6-7-6-7, though in fairness that's because it _is_ a quarry. All the diamonds that used to cover it have been mined out.
*   [Big Bad](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BigBad "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BigBad"): The Midnight entity manipulates the crew of the base into killing each other, and once again seeks to escape Midnight.
*   [Bittersweet Ending](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BittersweetEnding "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BittersweetEnding"): The Doctor kept his word and managed to get Aliss back home to her daughter. Unfortunately, [the Midnight entity](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination") has still managed to slaughter everyone at the base, including a majority of the rescue team, and it (or [another of its kind](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ThereIsAnother "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ThereIsAnother")) [may have](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding") latched onto someone aboard the ship leaving the planet... In the meantime, the Doctor and Belinda are not only no closer to getting back to Earth, but are now wondering if there's even an Earth for them to get back _to_ (at least after May 24, 2025).
*   [Bloodier and Gorier](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BloodierAndGorier "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BloodierAndGorier"): While still staying family friendly by not showing any injuries or faces, while exploring the mining colony, multiple corpses are seen with even The Doctor commenting that every bone in the bodies of the entity victims has been broken. The deaths shown in the episode are also brutal, with troopers being flung across the room and breaking their bones, and one shot of a trooper being flung into a wall head-first, then his corpse falling to the ground.
*   [The Bus Came Back](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBusCameBack "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBusCameBack"): After waiting 400,000 years in-universe and 17 years out, the entity from [Midnight has returned to terrorise The Doctor once more.](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight")
*   [Call-Back](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CallBack "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CallBack"):
    *   This isn't the first time Fifteen has foiled an [Eldritch abomination](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination") by [reflecting their own power back at them](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireofDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireofDeath"): Sutekh's Death Wave was undone in a similar fashion at the end of the previous series.
    *   [Once again](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux"), The Doctor and Belinda dress for their adventure by running into the depths of the Tardis before appearing through another doorway in new outfits.
    *   This is not [Britney Spears' ''Toxic'''s first time](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E2TheEndOfTheWorld "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E2TheEndOfTheWorld") on _Doctor Who_.
    *   An [eldritch abomination](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination") from the latter half of the revival's fourth series is [hiding behind someone's back, and can only be fleetingly glimpsed](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E11TurnLeft "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E11TurnLeft").
    *   [The creature seems to be just visible out of the corner of the eye](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E1TheEleventhHour "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E1TheEleventhHour").
    *   Much like Thirteen in [''It Takes You Away''](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS37E9ItTakesYouAway "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS37E9ItTakesYouAway"), the Doctor attempts to use a person's disability to smuggle information to his companion without them knowing. However, Aliss quickly calls him out on this, pointing out that she can lip read.
*   [Call a Rabbit a "Smeerp"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CallARabbitASmeerp "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CallARabbitASmeerp"): The soldiers refer to the facility as a mine for “Carbon 46”, with them not clarifying that it’s another name for diamonds until much later down the line, which helps make [The Reveal](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheReveal "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheReveal") hit that much harder.
*   [Cassandra Truth](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CassandraTruth "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CassandraTruth"): The troopers naturally find it hard to believe that the Doctor fought the monster 400,000 years ago. This was actually the last straw for Cassio, who immediately mutinies and takes matters into his own hands.
*   [Chekhov's Gun](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ChekhovsGun "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ChekhovsGun"):
    *   The mercury pipe feeding the well turns out to be key to freeing Aliss Fenly from the grip of the entity.
    *   Shaya's precision marksmanship is used to get the entity to move from Belinda to Shaya herself.
    *   It's possible to use a speech-to-text device that someone else is wearing. Shaya exploits this function to get Aliss to turn around and send the creature after Cassio.
*   [Cruel and Unusual Death](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CruelAndUnusualDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CruelAndUnusualDeath"): How The Midnight entity chooses to kill its victims this time if their compatriots don't shoot them first, violently throwing them around like a ragdoll.
*   [Darker and Edgier](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DarkerAndEdgier "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DarkerAndEdgier"): Similar to its [predecessor story](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight"), this story is quite a bit darker and scarier than the average _Doctor Who_ episode, being more violent, featuring elements of strong [Psychological Horror](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PsychologicalHorror "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PsychologicalHorror"), and the companion being [shot in the heart](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GodzillaThreshold "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GodzillaThreshold").
*   [Disability Aid Loss](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DisabilityAidLoss "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DisabilityAidLoss"): [Exploited](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Exploited "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Exploited") by most characters, who frequently turn off their "subtitle holograms" to obfuscate their words from Aliss, who is deaf. [She can still lip-read, though](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DefiedTrope "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DefiedTrope").
*   [Disability Immunity](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DisabilityImmunity "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DisabilityImmunity"): The entity whispers to its hosts and drives them homicidally insane, forcing others to kill them in self-defence, at which point it possesses the killer instead. Aliss is the only exception, with the Doctor theorising that her deafness meant that she couldn't hear the whispering.
*   [Dolled-Up Installment](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DolledUpInstallment "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DolledUpInstallment"): Behind the scenes, this was not originally written as a "[Midnight](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight")" sequel, which is why the creature's abilities are different. [Russell T Davies](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RussellTDavies "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RussellTDavies")'s writing credit is presumably for adapting it to fit with his episode.
*   [Dug Too Deep](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DugTooDeep "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DugTooDeep"): Digging for mercury on the burnt-out remains of a planet utterly hostile to all living things, the miners woke up something they shouldn't have, and it killed them all.
*   [Eldritch Abomination](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EldritchAbomination"): The Midnight entity is, again, incomprehensible, unstoppable and driving people mad.
*   [Enhance Button](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EnhanceButton "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EnhanceButton"): The Doctor's sonic screwdriver acts as one when viewing the base's camera footage.
*   [Face Death with Dignity](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FaceDeathWithDignity "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FaceDeathWithDignity"): Shaya sets a new high bar via [falling into the Well to imprison the Midnight entity](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide") once again. Unfortunately, it might have been [all for nought](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SenselessSacrifice "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SenselessSacrifice") in the end.
*   [Five-Second Foreshadowing](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FiveSecondForeshadowing "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FiveSecondForeshadowing"): Mere moments before the [Wham Line](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine") listed below, Shaya refers to Planet 6-7-6-7's star as previously being "Xtonic", a term which has only showed up in one previous context. In fact, for some viewers, _this_ was the true [Wham Line](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine"), as there is only one reason that term would be brought up in an episode...
*   [Flashback](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Flashback "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Flashback"): When the Doctor realizes this is Midnight and states he's been here before, footage from that episode (Ten interacting with the possessed Sky) is replayed. This has the benefit of reminding old _Doctor Who_ viewers which episode "The Well" is a sequel to and establishing the broad strokes for newer viewers who missed the Tenth Doctor era.
*   [Foreshadowing](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Foreshadowing "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Foreshadowing"):
    *   Prior to the episode's airing, the [title reveal![Image 2](https://static.tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pub/external_link.gif)](https://youtu.be/-ptkWfvgg78?si=dhl_kbAi6rLSikqM&t=50) had the detail of a digital clock hitting [midnight](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StealthSequel "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StealthSequel") before being covered by a bunker door.
    *   A very subtle one for only the most eagle-eyed viewers of the episodes from over a decade prior. Planet 6767 is stated to be bathed in "galvanic radiation" which kills anything and can leave a lingering contamination on what it touches. Apart from the incident with the Toymaker, the only other time that the term "galvanic radiation" was used in _Doctor Who_ was a "blink and you'll miss it" moment back in "Midnight", when Professor Hobbes briefly described the Xtonic sunlight as a raw form of galvanic radiation.
    *   Even before the exact identity of the threat is made clear, the true threat of the episode is hinted at by the circumstances. A small group of people trapped on a planet that seemingly has no life due to being bathed in absolutely deadly radiation, and a couple of them catch split-second glimpses of a dark _thing_? Where have we heard that before...?
    *   After the Doctor and Belinda remove their armor, Cassio admonishes them because it's against regulation. Towards the end, the time it takes the Doctor and Belinda to put their armor back _on_ [helps the Midnight entity to catch up to the rest of the group](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NiceJobBreakingItHero "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NiceJobBreakingItHero"), though the delayed airlock certainly doesn't help.
    *   When the Doctor hugs Aliss (and therefore is looking at the space behind her,) he gets a quizzical look on his face, almost as if he can sense something is there.
    *   Shortly after the airlock door closes behind Aliss and two troopers, the screen shows that there are actually _four_ life forms inside.
*   [For the Evulz](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ForTheEvulz "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ForTheEvulz"): Once again, the Midnight entity torments a group of people into madness and death for no discernible reason. The Doctor wholly believes after how his last experience with the creature ended, possibly due to seeing into its mind when it stole his voice, that it torments others in the ways it does in large part just because it [gets a kick out of it](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Sadist "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Sadist").
*   [Godzilla Threshold](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GodzillaThreshold "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GodzillaThreshold"): Shaya shoots Belinda in the heart to get the entity to latch on to her, acknowledging that even if her aim is true and the shot doesn't outright kill her, she'll only have the slimmest chance of survival. Thankfully, due to futuristic medicine and the TARDIS, she gets better.
*   [Heroic Suicide](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide"): Shaya kills herself by throwing herself into the well after the entity latches on to her. Unfortunately, the entity [might](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding") well have escaped and latched onto someone else anyway.
*   [Hidden Agenda Villain](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HiddenAgendaVillain "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HiddenAgendaVillain"): Mrs. Flood shows up outside the 21st century again, this time as a superior in the Foundation the characters of the week work for. She confirms from Mo a sighting of the Doctor's Vindicator, apparently quite interested in seeing it in action for reasons unrevealed.
*   [Human Aliens](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAliens "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HumanAliens"): Aliss, the miners, and the troopers. Similar to "[Dot and Bubble](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E5DotAndBubble "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E5DotAndBubble")" from last series, they appear to have blue [Alien Blood](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AlienBlood "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AlienBlood") from their injuries. However, while it's assumed that they are descendants of humans, the Doctor and Belinda learn that they have no idea what Earth is or know of any of its superstitions, which they are unnerved by. It's not a case of [Future Imperfect](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FutureImperfect "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FutureImperfect") either.
*   [I Did What I Had to Do](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/IDidWhatIHadToDo "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/IDidWhatIHadToDo"): Shaya says as much about tricking Cassio into being killed, what with his seizing authority from her and getting several troops killed to confirm the entity's existence.
*   [Immediate Sequel](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ImmediateSequel "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ImmediateSequel"): The episode follows on right from the previous, with the Doctor and Belinda not having changed outfits.
*   [Improbable Aiming Skills](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ImprobableAimingSkills "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ImprobableAimingSkills"): Shaya is an excellent shot. When Belinda becomes the host of the Midnight entity, Shaya shoots her in the millimeters-wide spot in her chest that would have the entity latch onto her while avoiding Belinda's heart.
*   [In Spite of a Nail](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InSpiteOfANail "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InSpiteOfANail"): It's heavily implied that the future seen in this episode, unlike in "Midnight", is an alternate [Bad Future](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BadFuture "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BadFuture") where the Earth died in 2025 and thus humanity perished before it could ever take to the stars in full. Despite this, the diamond planet was still named Midnight in this timeline.
*   [Jerkass Has a Point](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JerkassHasAPoint "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JerkassHasAPoint"): Cassio's mutiny, though very poorly executed, stemmed from valid concerns. Aliss was the sole survivor of a massacre that left everyone else in the mining colony dead, while she displayed only minor injuries. He was right to be wary of his commander ignoring the increasingly odd behaviour from the Doctor, which culminates in the Doctor's outlandish claim that he visited Midnight 400,000 years prior.
*   [Jump Scare](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JumpScare "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JumpScare"): One that is genuinely startling because of how sudden it is, with absolutely no indication that one might be coming. When Belinda is talking to one of the troopers about the fact that she’s never heard of Earth or humanity, she turns to look at Aliss only for one hell of a [Scare Chord](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ScareChord "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ScareChord") to play as she glimpses something behind her for less than a split-second.
*   [Kick the Dog](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KickTheDog "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KickTheDog"): Cassio makes a point to turn his subtitle hologram back on as he gives the "If there's movement, shoot to kill" order to the troops standing near Aliss, for seemingly no other reason than just to make clear to Aliss that he has no qualms about killing her.
*   [Leitmotif](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Leitmotif "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Leitmotif"): "[Midnight![Image 3](https://static.tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pub/external_link.gif)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4G5BdTypWdI)" makes an appropriate return in this episode, utilized while the Doctor runs through corridors towards Aliss and the rest of the group just after the reveal, and most times when the Midnight Entity is dropping bodies.
*   [Logical Weakness](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LogicalWeakness "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LogicalWeakness"): The creature violently kills anything that moves behind its host's back while someone else is looking at the host from the front. So if there's a reflective surface squarely behind the host's back while you're looking at their front, then the entity will automatically attack itself from its reflection appearing behind the host. The entity's already aware of this weakness and broke the mirrors of the mine, but it's foiled when the troopers cause a makeshift waterfall of mercury.
*   [Mundanger](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Mundanger "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Mundanger"): Alongside the terror of a creature that kills suddenly and horrifically with no apparent motive, there's also the danger of soldiers getting increasingly panicked over the whole situation.
*   [The Nameless](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheNameless "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheNameless"): The entity, just like in its last outing, is only referred to with descriptors like "the thing behind Aliss' back", with the Doctor even saying that it has no name and no identity. Somewhat creepily, the credits only reveal that "IT HAS NO NAME".
*   [Never Speak Ill of the Dead](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NeverSpeakIllOfTheDead "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NeverSpeakIllOfTheDead"): Despite Cassio leading a mutiny against Shaya and getting most of their platoon needlessly killed, when Mo makes her report on the mission she recommends he receive recognition because "he tried his best" under the circumstances.
*   [Nothing Is Scarier](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NothingIsScarier "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NothingIsScarier"): While the entity from Midnight does display some new abilities, we the audience learn precious little about it that its first outing didn't already tell us. The Doctor appears to learn something from its whispers, but the audience never hears it.
*   [Oh, Crap!](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OhCrap "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OhCrap"): A glorious one when The Doctor realizes what planet they are on.
*   [Poor Communication Kills](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PoorCommunicationKills "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PoorCommunicationKills"): A justified variation. The Leisure Palace Company _did_ abandon Midnight as per Ten's recommendation. The problem is that this was 400,000 years ago. Between the passage of time, the death of Midnight's sun, and cosmic upheaval, those old warnings have since been long lost and/or forgotten. So, Colony Base 15 had no idea they were setting up shop on a prohibited planet hosting a [Sealed Evil in a Can](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SealedEvilInACan "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SealedEvilInACan") until they accidentally opened the can.
*   [Psychological Horror](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PsychologicalHorror "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PsychologicalHorror"): As you would expect when the [Midnight entity](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight") is about.
*   [Ret-Gone](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RetGone "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RetGone"): No one aside from the main characters remembers Earth. The Doctor indicates that it's abnormal and not the result of [Future Imperfect](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FutureImperfect "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FutureImperfect"). The situation is too dire to discuss this during the episode, but in the ending Belinda briefly panics about it.
*   [Sadistic Choice](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SadisticChoice "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SadisticChoice"): The entity forces one on its hosts and everyone around them: each host eventually either a) kills anyone who walks behind them or b) drives those around them to attempt to murder them. If they choose the latter, they become possessed themselves. Forcing the entity to release its host only works temporarily before it latches onto someone again, and [killing oneself](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSuicide") instead when possessed _seems_ like a valid [option](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeAThirdOption "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeAThirdOption"), but even this [might](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AmbiguousEnding") not be enough.
*   [Sequel Episode](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SequelEpisode "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SequelEpisode"): To "[Midnight](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight")", with the return of the titular planet and the Midnight entity.
*   [Shout-Out](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ShoutOut "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ShoutOut"):
    *   Multiple characters suggest dealing with the mining site on Planet 6767 / Midnight, [by nuking the site from orbit](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Film/Aliens "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Film/Aliens").
    *   Many to _[Star Trek](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Franchise/StarTrek "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Franchise/StarTrek")_. The [space marines](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpaceMarine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpaceMarine") wear jumpsuits under their armour with blocks of black and blue on the shoulders that look very similar to the uniforms in _[Star Trek: The Next Generation](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/StarTrekTheNextGeneration "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/StarTrekTheNextGeneration")_. The ending reveals that their leader's costume is colour-coded red, just like that series' captains. It's mentioned in the dialogue that they serve a "Foundation", which could be a reference to [the Asimov books](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Literature/FoundationSeries "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Literature/FoundationSeries"), but is probably just a Federation soundalike. The chevron logo on the armored vests' chests even looks like an upside-down Starfleet delta. The Doctor also says "Where light has not gone before", referencing the franchise's famous catchphrase "Where no man/no one has gone before".
*   [The Spook](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheSpook "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheSpook"): The viewer doesn't learn anything more about what the entity is. Even though it displays different powers and a different logic behind its behaviour than last time, the change is never addressed, and in fact the difference makes it _more_ difficult to figure out what the hell it is. We _do_ actually see _part of it_ it on-screen this time, but only through split-second partially-obscured glimpses; aside from the fact that it _does_ apparently have a physical form, we're no closer to answers.
*   [Stealth Sequel](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StealthSequel "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StealthSequel"): This episode's status as a [Sequel Episode](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SequelEpisode "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SequelEpisode") to "[Midnight](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight")" isn't revealed until halfway through, with the reveal itself resolving the mystery of what happened to the mining base which drives the first half of the episode.
*   [Taught by Experience](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TaughtByExperience "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TaughtByExperience"): Zigzagged with the Doctor once he realizes what’s actually going on and what planet this is. Having encountered the Midnight entity before, the Doctor knows now what they’re up against and what didn’t work last time (on top of having hundreds of additional years' experience under his belt thanks to his subsequent incarnations). On the other hand, the Midnight entity remains one of _the_ most dangerous and abnormal lifeforms the Doctor’s ever encountered; all that additional experience can only compensate up to a point, especially since the entity itself uses [a very different set of abilities](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiscardAndDraw "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DiscardAndDraw") than the last time the Doctor dealt with it.
*   [Title Drop](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TitleDrop "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TitleDrop"):
    *   The Doctor watches security footage before almost everyone on the base was killed.**Base Commander**: It's behind you! From the well! It came out of the well!
        
    *   Later, Aliss says the same thing thing about the creature.**Aliss**: Something came out of the well. That's what they said. It came out of the well.
        
    *   The story this one is a sequel to is also name-dropped (even though it's been already mentioned in the dialogue).**The Doctor**: (referring to people getting killed behind Aliss) If this was a clock, you die at midnight.
        
*   [The Un-Reveal](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheUnreveal "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheUnreveal"): The cinematography deliberately keeps the true form of the Midnight entity a mystery to preserve the horror of the original story. The audience only see a dark shape in the shadows but can't make out a definite form. All we can infer, from the Doctor's and the doomed soldiers' reactions to looking at the thing, is that it is _[very](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeOurWordForIt "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeOurWordForIt")_ [unpleasant](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeOurWordForIt "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeOurWordForIt") to look at.
*   [Wham Line](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine"):
    *   This exchange between the Doctor and Shaya reveals to the audience and the Doctor that everyone is in great danger.**Shaya**: The entire surface of this planet was once made out of diamonds.  
        **The Doctor**: [What?](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FlatWhat "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FlatWhat") What is this planet called?  
        **Shaya**: 6-7-6-7.  
        **The Doctor**: The old name. 400,000 years ago, what was the planet called?  
        **Shaya**: It was called [Midnight](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS30E10Midnight").
        
    *   When the Doctor looks behind Aliss' back to talk to the Midnight entity, it whispers something to him that rattles him to his core:**The Doctor**: It knows my name.
        
*   [Wham Shot](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamShot "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamShot"): The survivors of the mission are reporting to Mrs. Flood at the end, who once again reveals that she's outside 21st century Earth (hell, outside of Earth in general).
*   [You Are Number Six](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouAreNumberSix "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouAreNumberSix"): [Troopers 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RedShirt "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RedShirt") aren't named at all. [Not even](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SubvertedTrope "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SubvertedTrope") in [the script](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AllThereInTheManual "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AllThereInTheManual").
*   [You Cannot Grasp the True Form](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouCannotGraspTheTrueForm "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouCannotGraspTheTrueForm"): [Zig-Zagged](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ZigZagged "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ZigZagged") by the entity itself. While it does have a comprehensible form, which both the Doctor and the soldiers it kills look at and [are universally horrified by](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeOurWordForIt "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TakeOurWordForIt"), it's obscured from the audience and even, to some extent, from most of the characters during the story's runtime. The behind-the-scenes featurette shows creature performer [Paul Kasey](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/PaulKasey "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/PaulKasey") in a costume with a round, black, vaguely insectoid head, but this probably isn't meant to be the "canon" appearance of the entity, since so much effort is put into obscuring its appearance onscreen. It's more likely designed in such a way as to create a bulky, black shape designed to freak the viewer out when seen for a split second.
*   [You Kill It, You Bought It](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouKillItYouBoughtIt "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouKillItYouBoughtIt"): The entity latches onto the person who kills its host. Possibly Subverted if it actually faked a transference from a mortally wounded Belinda to Shaya and instead latched onto Mo with none aware until after the Doctor and Belinda left.

* * *

_"I don't think I know anything any more."_
